comment: The decisive correction is A<C: the narrower two-layer GRU beats the wider single-layer GRU at AdamW lr .003 for 512 steps. I overextended a shallow/wide optimization preference into this well-trained regime. Reduced fitting of irrelevant history is plausible, but gold alone cannot establish that mechanism. K1017 helped rank the transformers; K1075 does not resolve the GRU pair. History contains five comparable equal-rate, ordinally resolved GRU comparisons: narrower/deeper wins only once, at 1024 steps. Matched adaptive lab comparisons favor narrower/equal-width deeper GRUs in only 2/23 pairs, all at nominal exposure below .5; none cover this question’s 1.536. Thus no tested general reversal rule is supported.

explanation: B is the best bet for test cross-entropy: its small learning rate allows gradual fitting of the two-coordinate boundary over 2048 steps while limiting aggressive fitting of irrelevant features. A learns faster, but its modest decoupled decay may not offset poorer held-out confidence after prolonged training. C’s still larger rate and zero decay increase that risk. This is a recipe-specific judgment, not a universal low-rate rule. <cited>K1001,K1005,K1073,K1116</cited>
comment: The same architecture made optimizer trajectory the deciding factor. At 2048 steps and batch 16, the conservative AdamW recipe B beat both faster recipes on held-out CE. K1001 and K1073 helped prevent maximum-displacement selection; K1116 supported considering long-budget rate reversals but did not directly predict B, since its lowest tested rate lost on a different recipe. The result establishes this full-recipe ordering, not a rate-only effect: learning rate, beta2 and decay also differ. Irrelevant-feature fitting and confidence inflation remain hypotheses, not measured mechanisms. No new general rule was tested.

The missed comparisons were B>A and E>D. I overextended K1071’s local bigram displacement band into a GRU rate ceiling; this narrow GRU instead benefited from lr=.003 at 256 steps. I also imposed an Adam preference where K1002 explicitly calls a 10× Adagrad/Adam rate ratio mixed; E’s nominal progress (.096) slightly exceeds D’s (.0768). Faster fitting is plausible, but parameter motion was not measured. Backtesting found Adagrad winning 2/3 matching history comparisons across two questions; the sole matching .003-versus-.001 GRU comparison favored .001 at 512 steps. The lab contained no exact same-model plain-CE pairs for either contrast. K1001/K1012 warned against both extrapolations. No general full-ranking rule is established.

A beat E despite having fewer LayerNorm blocks. I over-weighted K1006’s normalization-count tendency: A’s terminal-normalized plain GELU recipe outperformed E’s residual SiLU recipe with an unnormalized final block. Terminal normalization could preserve useful feature scale after A’s contracting plain stack, but the revealed ranking does not establish that mechanism. Backtesting terminal-only-LN smooth plain models against smooth residual models with at least as many LNs gave 1/3 wins in decisive history comparisons; the lab had only one comparable pair, a win under RMSprop, none under Adagrad. Conversely, more-LN smooth Adagrad recipes won 7/7 broader lab pairs. K1074 supported C; K1006 was misleading when promoted from a tendency into the A/E ordering. No general override is validated.

explanation: C should win: its shallow SiLU network and fast AdamW updates can learn the multiplicative boundary within 512 steps. A's much smaller learning rate and deeper rectifier network leave it comparatively undertrained. B's tiny momentum-SGD rate provides still less effective progress. C's high rate carries fitting risk, but the tabular evidence does not justify rejecting it solely for large nominal displacement.
comment: C won through substantially faster adaptive learning combined with a shallow smooth network suited to nonlinear tabular interactions. A's low-rate deep Adam recipe and B's very low-rate momentum SGD were comparatively undertrained. K1003 and K1012 supported the progress comparison; K1009 and K1056 supplied scoped architecture preferences. K1073 helped avoid treating C's large nominal displacement as an automatic long-budget failure. This outcome reinforces existing conditional evidence rather than establishing a new rate threshold or architecture rule.

Identical architectures made optimizer progress the main discriminator. The shallow normalized multivariate MLP remained undertrained at the conservative rates: RMSprop .001 ranked first, followed by RMSprop .0001 and Adam .0001. Adagrad .0003 narrowly preceded AdamW .00003, consistent with approximate cumulative progress of .0096 versus .00768. K1001, K1002, and K1070 helped; K1004 and K1012 appropriately limited confidence in maximum-progress and close-progress comparisons. This outcome does not establish a universal RMSprop advantage or validate displacement as a complete ranking rule.

B’s advantage over A and E decided the error: I treated its deep, sparsely normalized GELU stack as necessarily undertrained. The gold shows that penalty was too strong at AdamW lr×steps=.0512; it does not establish why B won. K1006’s normalization tendency was overextended into a deterministic ranking; K1008 helped correctly place C ahead of D. Backtesting rejects a general “promote B-like networks” correction: comparable deep plain smooth one-LN candidates won 0/10 comparisons against normalized deep residuals and 0/12 against shallow residuals across four lab sets, mostly SGD. Nearby history q_0f0256 also ranked its B-like candidate last. No tested general mechanism explains this target/budget-specific reversal.

explanation: B is favored: its terminal-normalized plain network can learn successive nonlinear transformations without preserving the input through every block. At this short, low-rate AdamW budget, spiral evidence supports such plain architectures over residual alternatives. A’s extra normalization is not a reliable advantage under adaptive optimization; C’s ReLU skips likewise offer no clear benefit over B’s smooth, normalized composition.
comment: B’s terminal-normalized plain architecture was the useful discriminator among identical low-rate AdamW recipes. K1061 supported this choice through its spiral Adam-family evidence favoring terminal-LN plain networks, while K1125 warned that additional normalization need not help residual networks under low-rate Adam. A’s extra LN and C’s residual ReLU structure therefore did not establish an advantage. K1001 helped avoid inventing an optimizer-progress difference where all recipes shared the same rate and budget. This gold result supports the scoped preference, but does not isolate skips, activation, or LN count as its cause.

The missed comparison was B versus A. I overvalued A’s three early LayerNorms and presumed its small initial logits would beat B’s low-rate Adagrad. A’s two unnormalized terminal GELU blocks plausibly attenuate useful features and SGD gradients; B’s shallower adaptive network avoids that particular bottleneck. K1059/K1061 warned about SGD tail placement, while K1012 explicitly rejects initialization-based ordering at low progress. Lab checks found terminal LN better in 12/12 matched-shape, equal-LN SGD contrasts across eight spiral sets, but these test placement, not B versus A. Exact comparable cross-optimizer pairs numbered zero in both history and lab. Thus the mechanism remains plausible, not established; no tested general rule warrants promotion.

I over-weighted feed-forward width and under-weighted depth: B’s four layers beat E’s three and D’s two; C also beat D despite its smaller feed-forward block. Adagrad’s nominal progress is only 0.00096, so initialization and architecture-dependent early learning plausibly dominate, but their causal contributions remain unmeasured. Historical shared-rate Adagrad≤1e-4 comparisons favored deeper equal-width transformers 5/5 across three questions, wider equal-depth transformers 3/3, and GRUs 12/12. The lab supplied no comparable tiny-Adagrad depth pairs; low-progress SGD depth comparisons were mixed (4/8). K1002/K1012 helped identify this regime. I misapplied K1017’s feed-forward preference across depths and treated K1068’s mixed width evidence as grounds to place C last. No validated complete-order rule emerged.

explanation: C has the strongest effective training progress: AdamW’s lr×steps is 0.1536, versus B’s 0.01536 and A’s Adagrad estimate of about 0.0045. Its two later LayerNorm blocks support fitting the nonlinear target. B’s extra normalization and rectifier activation are useful, but likely cannot compensate for its tenfold lower learning rate. A’s residual connections likewise cannot overcome its very conservative Adagrad updates.
comment: I mistook nominal displacement for decisive learning progress. B’s early normalization and LeakyReLU plausibly preserve input-dependent features better than C’s unnormalized GELU prefix, despite its lower rate; this mechanism is not isolated by the gold result. K1006 supported reconsidering normalization; I overextended K1012’s progress tendency and K1002’s same-architecture scope. History q_6845b5 uses identical recipes and budget but favors C on another target: the proposed B-over-C rule scored 0/1 historical checks. Broader lab comparisons favored lower-rate, more-normalized rectifiers in 18/28 pairs across 21 sets, but none matched both deep plain architectures. Thus the evidence establishes a target/split-dependent recipe reversal, not a validated general winner rule.

All five choices share the exact network, so optimizer progress under the short budget decided the ranking. AdamW at 1e-4 outpaced the conservative adaptive alternatives; low-rate RMSprop beat Adagrad, whose learning rate was only three times AdamW’s. Momentum SGD made more progress than tiny-rate plain SGD, but both remained behind the adaptive choices. K1001, K1002, K1003, and K1019 supported these comparisons. K1070 supplied limited supporting context for RMSprop in classification, not a direct RMSprop-versus-Adagrad rule. This result adds no new general rule.

The missed comparison was D versus E. D combines residual paths and three LNs; E has two LNs followed by two unnormalized plain blocks. Better signal propagation is a plausible explanation for D’s advantage, but the revealed ranking does not isolate that mechanism. I overapplied K1039’s one-LN activation preference; K1006 explicitly cautions against deterministic LN/activation rankings across residual and tail changes. Backtesting smooth residual versus rectifier plain regression candidates with one extra LN and shared SGD rate/momentum found smooth wins in 7/12 decidable historical comparisons, losing 5. Lab analogues favored smooth in 2/2 sets, but neither matched E’s deep two-block tail or this tiny rate. No general override is validated.

explanation: A offers the best balance of learning speed and generalization for this small bigram dataset. Its RMSprop rate permits meaningful fitting within 256 steps. B’s tiny Adagrad rate produces far less progress and likely underfits. C learns faster, but its much larger cumulative update scale risks fitting sampling noise; same-model small-GRU evidence favors more moderate rates over aggressive ones.
comment: C’s advantage is consistent with faster learning of the stronger token-conditioned signal, not a demonstrated universal optimizer advantage. Nominal progress is A=.0768, B=.00096, C=.768; B is severely undertrained. I misapplied K1071’s moderate-progress warning to A, whose progress is below .1; its full evidence actually favors larger updates in that regime. K1001/K1002 helped, but do not prove C wins. Crucially, q_4fa7b4 uses identical recipes and chooses A at alpha=.8, whereas this alpha=1.4 instance chooses C. Thus my asserted sampling-noise mechanism was unsupported; target strength and full-recipe interactions matter.
hypothesis:
Provisional rule: for same-architecture width64 GRU bigram LMs, plain CE, 800 training windows, T256–1024, and alpha≥1, prefer an Adam/AdamW/RMSprop candidate with nominal Δ=lr·T in [.1,1] over another with Δ in [.03,.1), provided the increase is at least 2×. This predicts C over A here; tiny-rate Adagrad B remains an undertraining concern.

Mechanism hypothesis: stronger transition contrasts require more optimization before token-conditioned predictions are learned; the smaller-rate candidate remains insufficiently fitted. Parameter motion and training CE were not measured, so this mechanism is unconfirmed.

History backtest, excluding this revealed question: 5 resolvable pairs across 4 questions, 5 hits, 0 misses. At alpha=.8, the same higher-progress preference achieves only 2/6; one additional alpha=1.4 comparison is unresolved because neither candidate won.

Lab backtest, matching model and comparing only within sets: alpha≥1 gives 6/6 higher-progress wins, but all reuse one alpha=1.4 dataset. Across all alpha values, the rule gives 9/9 across only two sets. With the smaller candidate already at Δ=.1–.3, higher progress wins only 1/5 across three sets. These are dependent comparisons, not independent replications. The alpha boundary is tentative: the alpha=.8 lab set also favors higher progress, so alpha alone cannot explain the reversal.

comment: B’s moderate-rate GRU was the strongest fit for the bigram task. D’s shallow, wider transformer ranked ahead of the deeper, narrower E/C pair; E’s beta2=.95 recipe edged C’s beta2=.999 recipe. A’s RMSprop rate produced nominal displacement 1.536, versus B’s .1536, making excessive fitting a relevant risk rather than a progress advantage. K1071 supported this caution, K1124 supplied nearby GRU-versus-transformer shape evidence, and K1005 kept minor optimizer differences as weak tie-breakers. None alone establishes the complete order: K1124 does not directly cover these optimizer/batch combinations, and nominal displacement is only a proxy. No new tested general rule emerged.

The decisive miss was C versus A: identical architecture, optimizer, and budget, but GELU beat ReLU. I over-applied K1008’s rectifier preference as a deterministic tie-break. The revealed ranking establishes an activation effect here, not its mechanism; smoother feature evolution under small Adam updates is plausible but unverified. Backtesting found no exact ReLU/GELU architecture-and-optimizer twins in multivariate lab data. Broader equal-LN, shared-optimizer/rate comparisons at Adam-family Δ<0.1 favored smooth activations in only 3/6 pairs across five sets. Two exact historical activation comparisons favored ReLU, but used Adagrad/SGD, not Adam. Thus no tested GELU override is justified. K1006/K1074 helped rank normalized depth; K1008 misled through overconfidence, not a universally false claim.

explanation: B is my prediction: its small adaptive updates have 2048 steps to learn the simple interaction boundary while limiting aggressive fitting of the 13 irrelevant features. A’s much larger rate risks poorer held-out confidence after repeated exposure; C increases that risk further with the highest rate and no decay. This is a recipe-specific judgment, not a universal preference for low learning rates.
comment: I over-weighted speculative overconfidence and distractor fitting. A provides substantially more learning progress than B; C shows that maximizing rate is not sufficient either. The revealed winner supports this balance, but does not isolate why C loses. Backtesting same-model Adam-family comparisons with ≥10× rate gaps: higher rate won 9/11 historical pairs; shallow sparse-interaction models won 1/1 historical pair and 5/5 lab pairs across five sets. Deep sparse models reversed this tendency, winning 0/4 lab pairs. These comparisons are dependent and not exact replications. K1073 and K1116 explicitly reject blanket long-budget low-rate preference; they did not mislead me. I ignored their scope warnings and misapplied K1001’s saturation caveat.

The ranking followed the large progress gaps, with architecture informing the leading pair: C's normalized residual depth was favored over A's shallow zero-LN network, while both had substantially stronger optimization than E, D, and B. E's Adagrad progress estimate exceeded those of the two plain-SGD candidates; D's tenfold SGD learning-rate advantage over B outweighed B's rectifier activation. K1001, K1002, K1003, and K1012 helped calibrate these gaps. K1080 cautioned against treating normalized depth as an automatic multivariate winner, so C over A remained the least certain comparison. No new general rule was established.

A versus E decided the error: identical recipes except activation, and ReLU beat LeakyReLU(0.01). I assumed improved negative-side gradient flow would help; that was unsupported. Hard gating might help isolate XOR sign regions, but the gold provides no causal evidence or loss margin. K1018/K1065 supported low-dimensional depth considerations; K1016 discouraged capacity-based ranking. None establishes LeakyReLU superiority. Backtesting found no activation-only matched pairs in 107 historical XOR questions or the lab. Architecture-confounded, same-optimizer-type/rate comparisons favored ReLU in 32/72 historical pairs and 8/18 lab pairs; low-dimensional lab results were 4/7 versus 4/11 at ≥8 features. These mixed results do not justify a new activation rule.

explanation: B is the strongest choice: Adam provides coordinate-wise adaptation, while two normalized LeakyReLU blocks support efficient regression fitting. A’s momentum makes it competitive, but its extra residual block offers no clear advantage at this short budget. C preserves input scale without normalization, but its smooth, unnormalized stack is less likely to learn the polynomial’s variation as efficiently as B.
comment: A’s win is consistent with momentum exploiting coherent gradients from the positive, nonoscillatory polynomial, while residual paths preserve input-dependent signal. This mechanism remains unmeasured. I wrongly treated Adam’s coordinate adaptation as a decisive advantage: K1019 makes A competitive, and K1012 explicitly rejects an adaptive tie-break at comparable progress. K1006/K1008 did not resolve A versus B across optimizer/residual changes. Crucially, q_6af0d0 uses identical recipes on an oscillatory target and favors B. A blanket momentum preference hits only 1/2 comparable historical questions. Lab filtering found two near-parity normalized-rectifier comparisons, both favoring momentum, but neither matched residual-versus-plain architectures. Evidence is insufficient for a general target-dependent rule.

The decisive error was placing low-rate AdamW A above both RMSprop candidates. K1057’s broad univariate Adam preference was overapplied; K1001/K1012 caution against converting nominal progress into a total order. RMSprop’s initially uncorrected second-moment accumulator plausibly accelerates early fitting at 3e-5, but this mechanism is not measured here. Historical same-model, equal-rate comparisons favor RMSprop in 3/4 questions at 3e-5, including both T256 questions; Adam wins the remaining T512 comparison. Lab equal-rate T256 comparisons favor RMSprop in 15/25 pairs across 12 sets, but none match architectures. At .001/.003, RMSprop wins only 4/23 and 0/14. This supports a low-rate exception, not a reliable replacement rule. E-first and C-last were correct.

Shared momentum SGD made activation and signal propagation decisive. K1039 favored A’s LeakyReLU over C’s SiLU at equal LN count. K1074 and K1006 supported normalized deep C over shallow E, although this remains a bundled architecture preference. E’s normalization and short path favored it over zero-LN D. B’s five plain SiLU blocks, with only an initial LN, made it the strongest undertraining risk; D’s residual paths supported D over B, consistent with K1015’s conditional guidance. No new general rule was established or backtested.

explanation: B offers the best balance of fitting speed and stability for this wide post-LN transformer. Its AdamW rate should learn the shared bigram law within 256 steps. C updates ten times more slowly and is likely to remain undertrained; A’s aggressive RMSprop rate risks degrading fitting in this wide architecture, so its larger nominal progress is not an advantage.
comment: C’s conservative recipe wins despite nominal Δ=.00768; I wrongly equated its tenfold smaller update budget with undertraining. Whether this reflects better optimization or generalization is unresolved: gold alone cannot establish overfitting or instability. K1001/K1071 warned against that inference; K1102 supported caution about aggressive wide-transformer RMSprop but did not settle B versus C. Backtesting a same-shape, width128 conservative-Adam preference found two historical comparisons: one hit, one miss. Crucially, q_c9b76f uses byte-identical recipes and favors B at α=1.0 on another split. Model-matched lab Adam-family comparisons with ≥3× rate separation favor lower rates in 1/1 width128 pair, versus 35/102 width64 and 0/55 width32 pairs. Evidence is insufficient for an α threshold or universal low-rate rule.

B’s residual LeakyReLU network with two LayerNorm blocks beat D’s plain GELU network with only early normalization. Better preservation of input-dependent nonlinear features is plausible, but gold alone does not isolate the mechanism. I overweighted D’s approximately 3.8× nominal displacement advantage (.0512 versus .0136). K1002 is same-architecture evidence; applying it here exceeded scope. K1006 and K1012 warned against that extrapolation; K1008’s equal-LN activation evidence cannot establish this comparison either. A proposed “extra-normalized rectifier Adagrad beats smooth Adam despite 2–10× lower displacement” rule failed all five lab comparisons across three sets. History supplied zero matching comparisons, and the exact architectural scope had no lab matches. No general rule is supported.

K1039 supported placing the rectifier candidates above the smooth candidates under shared low-rate plain SGD. K1006 supported C’s three-LN advantage, while K1016 discouraged ranking by width alone. The remaining ordering was architectural judgment: D’s residual path and terminal LN favored it over E; A’s residual path plausibly enabled faster mean fitting than B’s plain SiLU stack with an unnormalized tail, despite B’s extra LN. Those explanations are consistent with the gold order but are not isolated causal evidence. No new general rule was tested.

explanation: C provides enough adaptive optimization to learn the bigram law, with a moderate learning-rate budget (0.1536). A’s larger RMSprop budget (0.512) is less favorable for this small GRU: more parameter movement need not improve held-out cross-entropy once fitting is adequate. B’s low-rate plain SGD makes much slower progress and is likely to remain undertrained.
comment: A’s RMSprop recipe fits the bigram law better than C’s slower AdamW recipe; B’s low-rate plain SGD remains undertrained. I incorrectly treated K1071’s historical displacement band as a ceiling and assumed C had adequate fitting without evidence. K1001 explicitly warns against that inference; K1019 correctly disfavors B. A matched lab comparison using the exact A/C optimizer configurations favors A at 256 steps (CE 2.69138 versus 2.94892). Faster fitting is a plausible explanation, but parameter motion and convergence were not measured.
hypothesis:
Provisional rule: for same-architecture, nonresidual width64 GRU bigram LMs with one or two layers, plain CE, 800 training windows, and 256–512 steps, prefer RMSprop at lr 0.0003–0.001 over Adam/AdamW at least 3× slower. Do not reject RMSprop merely because lr×steps exceeds 0.3.

History backtest: three qualifying pairwise comparisons across two questions, three hits and zero misses: q_b7578f supplies two dependent RMSprop-versus-AdamW wins; q_aa66e7 supplies one. Lab backtest: three comparisons across three sets, three wins, median RMSprop/AdamW CE ratio 0.932. The exact focal optimizer contrast appears in one lab set, ratio 0.913.

Hypothesized mechanism: the faster adaptive recipe reduces finite-budget fitting error sufficiently to outweigh any late-fitting penalty. This is not measured mechanistically and has limited independent support. Scope excludes lr 0.003: nearby history reverses at that rate, including identical recipes winning with RMSprop in q_f5aefa but Adam in q_ae5159. No universal RMSprop superiority or displacement ceiling follows.

comment: All candidates share the same model, so optimizer progress dominated: B’s Adam rate gives substantially more progress over 256 steps than A/E, followed by D and low-rate Adagrad C. K1001 and K1002 supported this ordering. K1005 appropriately treated AdamW versus Adam at identical rates as a weak tie-break; E beating A is consistent with that preference but does not establish a general decoupled-decay advantage. No new tested hypothesis emerged.

The missed comparisons were B<C<D: four heads beat two, and FF64 beat FF128. At Adam lr×steps=.00768, initialization and early optimization may dominate these small architecture differences, but the revealed ordering does not establish a mechanism. K1017 helped place A but misled my FF ranking; I overextended K1069’s head preference. Low-rate history favored larger FF in 6/6 comparisons and two heads in 2/2, but none used width32. Matched lab head comparisons split 3/6 at low rates across two sets, versus 0/6 larger-head wins at high rates; no matched low-rate FF pairs existed. Thus the backtest does not support a general reversal rule predicting this gold answer.

explanation: C is favored because AdamW generally fits univariate regression better than RMSprop on the identical network, including when RMSprop uses a higher learning rate. A lacks that optimizer advantage; B's larger RMSprop rate is not reliably beneficial and often worsens test MSE in wide univariate networks. C's small weight decay is unlikely to outweigh this advantage over 512 steps.
comment: B’s win contradicts my blanket AdamW preference: at 512 steps, RMSprop 1e-4 evidently benefits this four-cycle target more than either 3e-5 recipe. Faster acquisition of oscillatory structure is plausible, but the revealed winner alone cannot establish that mechanism. K1057 and K1063 misled when treated as decisive; K1001 correctly warns that optimizer preferences are conditional. Historical same-architecture comparisons with RMSprop rate ≥ Adam-family rate favored RMSprop in 16/21 pairs across 13 questions. However, mixed-architecture lab comparisons favored RMSprop only 99/214 times, including 70/139 oscillatory pairs; no exact-model optimizer controls were available. These checks reject categorical AdamW dominance but do not validate a general rule predicting B.

The sole error was B versus C: two transformer layers beat one despite identical width, heads, feedforward size, optimizer, and budget. I overextended K1017’s shallow-depth tendency into a definite ordering at Δ=.512. An extra block may improve current-token extraction from token-plus-position embeddings, but the revealed ranking does not establish that mechanism. Backtesting found five matched one-versus-two-layer history comparisons: deeper won four, all outside this Adam regime. Finite matched lab comparisons favored deeper at Δ=.0256 but shallower in both Δ=.256 tests; none matched this narrow, decay-regularized Δ=.512 setup. K1075 helped select A. No tested general rule supports reversing B/C here.
